summary: Fortune reports that U.S. existing-home sales fell 15% year over year in September 2023 to 3.96 million, the lowest in 13 years, as mortgage rates hit 8%, inventory shrank and prices kept rising. The article argues the market resembles the 1980s rather than 2008, with millennials entering homebuying age amid aggressive Fed rate hikes. Experts say affordability is worse than at the 2006 peak and the rate lock-in effect keeps owners from selling.
one_line: Existing-home sales hit a 13-year low in September 2023 as 8% mortgage rates and scarce inventory freeze the market in a pattern echoing the 1980s.
key_facts: Existing-home sales dropped 15% year over year in September 2023 to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.96 million, per the National Association of Realtors (NAR).
The 3.96 million figure is the lowest in 13 years, since 2010.
Mortgage rates hit 8% in the week of the article, a record for the 21st century.
Existing-home sales prices topped $306,000, a 5% increase since the year began, according to the Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index.
Housing inventory is down 8.1% from a year earlier, according to NAR.
Between September 2018 and September 2023, the average number of homes on the market fell 60% to fewer than 700,000 active listings, per Realtor.com.
Zillow warned in May that housing would enter a 'deep freeze' if a debt-limit default pushed mortgage rates to 8%; the default was averted but 8% rates arrived anyway.
In the 1980s, Fed Chair Paul Volcker fought inflation with rate hikes, and the average 30-year fixed mortgage peaked at about 18% by late 1981.
Existing-home sales dropped 50% from 1978 to 1982, according to the Office of Policy Development and Research.
Millennials buy about 60% of homes bought with mortgages in recent years, per Redfin.

Goldman Sachs managing director Roger Ashworth said affordability for the incremental buyer is worse than at the 2006 peak, and predicts home prices rising 1.8% by end of 2023 and 3.5% by end of 2024.
More than 90% of existing-home owners are locked into mortgage rates below 6%, according to First American's Odeta Kushi.
First American's Mark Fleming said today's market is not overbuilt or driven by loose lending, subprime mortgages or highly leveraged homeowners.
